Indelible means impossible to remove, erase, or forget. It describes something so permanent that no amount of effort, time, or force can wipe it away.

Think of it as the opposite of temporary. If something is indelible, it is there to stay — whether you like it or not.
Two Worlds Where This Word Lives

This word works in two different but closely related ways:

1. The Physical World — Things You Can Touch

In its more literal sense, indelible describes a physical mark or substance that cannot be washed off or removed.

You have likely seen the phrase "indelible ink" or "indelible marker." This is ink that, once it touches a surface, is permanent. You cannot scrub it away.

"She signed the contract in indelible ink, making it impossible to alter."

"The red dye left an indelible stain on the white shirt."

In this sense, the word is simply telling you: this mark is not going anywhere.

2. The World of the Mind and Heart — Things You Feel or Remember

This is where the word truly comes alive and where it is used most often in everyday language. Here, indelible describes an experience, memory, or impression that is burned so deeply into your mind or heart that you could never forget it — even if you tried.

"The death of his father left an indelible mark on him."

"Watching the first moonwalk on television was an indelible moment for an entire generation."

"Her kindness made an indelible impression on everyone who met her."

Notice the phrase "indelible mark" — it is the single most common way this word is used. Just like a permanent ink stain on fabric, an experience can leave a mark on a person's soul or memory that never fades.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

Here is something important: indelible is not a neutral word. It carries weight and intensity. When you describe something as indelible, you are communicating that it had a profound effect — something that shaped a person, a place, or a time in a way that could never be undone.

This means the word is used for both deeply beautiful experiences and deeply painful ones:

Beautiful:

"The birth of her daughter was the most indelible moment of her life."

Painful:

"The war left an indelible scar on the nation's history."

The word does not judge whether the permanence is good or bad. It simply says: this will not go away.
Degree of Permanence — Why "Indelible" Is a Strong Word

Many words describe things that last a long time — lasting, enduring, persistent, unforgettable. But indelible is stronger than most of them.

When you say something is lasting, you mean it continues for a long time.
When you say something is indelible, you are saying it is permanent, full stop. There is no "eventually it will fade." An indelible impression is one that stays for life — and sometimes, beyond one individual life, across history.

This is why the word is often used for:

  • Moments that define a person's identity
  • Historical events that changed the world
  • Emotional experiences so powerful they become a part of who someone is

Certain words appear with indelible very frequently. Knowing these pairings will help you recognise and use the word naturally:

  • Indelible mark — the most common pairing by far
  • Indelible impression — the effect someone or something has on your mind
  • Indelible memory — a memory you will carry forever
  • Indelible stain — a permanent blemish, physical or moral ("a scandal that left an indelible stain on his reputation")
  • Indelible impact — a lasting effect on something or someone
  • Indelible ink / indelible marker — a pen or ink that is permanent
Register and Tone — When to Use It

Indelible is a moderately formal word. You will find it often in:

  • Literature and serious writing
  • Journalism and speeches
  • Thoughtful conversation about meaningful experiences

You would not typically say to a friend, "That pizza was indelible!" — it would sound strange and overly dramatic for something casual. But you might say, "That trip to Japan left an indelible impression on me," and that would sound perfectly natural and expressive.

Reserve it for things that are genuinely significant and permanent in their impact.
A Quick Test to Know If You Are Using It Correctly

Before using indelible, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Is it permanent? Could it be erased, removed, or forgotten with time and effort? If yes, indelible is the wrong word. If no — if it truly cannot be undone or forgotten — then indelible fits perfectly.
  2. Does it carry weight? Is the thing you are describing significant, powerful, or deeply felt? Indelible is not a word for minor things. It belongs to experiences, marks, and moments that matter profoundly.

If the answer to both questions is yes, you are using the word correctly.

Indelible = impossible to remove or forget; permanently fixed in a surface, mind, or history.

The word is about permanence of the most absolute kind. Whether it is ink on paper or grief in the heart, if it is indelible, nothing will ever fully take it away. That is both what makes the word precise, and what gives it such quiet power.
